To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

NGC 6251 is a canonical example of an LERG; it has an X-ray spectrum that is dominated by a single power-law component of photon index 1.82; there are no signs of obscured, accreting X-ray emission from NGC 6251; and the luminosity of the accretion-related component must be substantially less than Eddington in nature, and therefore the accretion flow must be radiatively inefficient.
NGC 6251 is a low-excitation radio-galaxy with no evidence for an obscuring toroidal structure and that the accretion rate onto the supermassive black hole is likely to be radiatively inefficient.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the nature of the accretion flows in NGC 6251 and the origin of the X-ray emission.
understanding how the energy released in the accretion flow of a supermassive black hole is channeled into the formation of relativistic jets and the production of radio emission.
the X-ray properties of the LERG NGC 6251 and the nature of the accretion flow.

there is no evidence for an obscured accretion disc in NGC 625 1.
the X-ray emission from NGC 6251 can be explained by thermal emission from a hot gas in the host galaxy and its group-scale surroundings.
there are no signs of a standard accretion disk, or a torus, or a hot corona, or a warm absorber in the Suzaku spectrum of NGC 6251.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have not found evidence for a radiatively efficient accretion disc in NGC 6251, which is consistent with our previous work and with the hypothesis that NGC 6251 is a radiatively inefficient accretor.
NGC 6251 has a jet-dominated nucleus and is likely to be accreting in a radiatively weak mode.
NGC 6251 is a canonical LERG with no evidence for a torus and a low-luminosity, radiatively inefficient central engine.
The main takeaway from our work is that
LERGs are a class of radio galaxies that may lack a central accretion disk and may be accreting at low rates.
, despite the fact that NGC 6251 has a radio jet that is almost certainly more powerful than its X-ray emission, it does not have an obscured accretion component.
the Suzaku spectrum of NGC 6251 is consistent with that of a jet-dominated LERG, and is not consistent with the X-ray emission from an obscured, radiatively efficient AGN.
